Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Vignette:
Amir had been twenty when the violation occurred during a late-night audit review at a downtown hotel. He remembered the exact moment: a colleague stepping into the private office, the heavy door catching behind him, the sudden weight and grip that left him breathless. What haunted him most was not the physical act alone, but the quiet moral violation in the colleague’s demeanor afterward—a casual brush of the shoulder, a lack of apology that felt like erasure. For months following that night, Amir found himself caught in a slow unraveling. The scent of the hotel’s linen room, a sharp mix of starched cotton and citrus cologne, would suddenly seize him in the present, pulling him back to that locked door. He had come to believe that any room with that particular fragrance could become a trap. Around him, people misbehaved with a careless disregard that echoed his own experience; a dropped coffee cup left to stain a carpet, a coworker cutting in line without a glance—all felt like familiar reflections. When he heard others speak of his ex, how she had waited up for him that night or how she finally moved on, a cold knot formed in his chest, each mention a quiet reminder of the life that paused while he recovered. As the months passed, Amir’s days became a series of careful calculations. In his work as an auditor, where he spent his hours poring over ledgers and leading team reviews, he began to notice how easily he could be judged. Clients watched his posture, his juniors noted his clipped responses, and he would feel their eyes scanning him as though he were a document out of compliance. He had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation; the incident felt like an isolated flaw in his own judgment, not a circumstance anyone could have endured. He dressed in layers of charcoal and navy, tucking in his shirts, keeping his collar high and his sleeves long. The fabric softened the lines of his body and kept the room’s attention at a distance. In conference rooms and client offices, he always positioned himself near the door. It was not a conscious decision but a quiet certainty: if the space became too demanding, the exit was right there. He avoided unfamiliar restaurant blocks and new training centers for the same reason, unable to assess the danger until he could map the perimeter. When someone stepped quickly toward him or gestured with their hand, his shoulders would lock, his breath catching in a way that felt both sudden and entirely expected. His muscles remained perpetually wound, a quiet readiness that never fully settled, and his score of forty-three on the intake checklist simply mirrored what he had already known. By his twenty-second winter, his happiness, once a steady current in his life, had dulled into a quiet, persistent weight. He looked back at photographs from before the audit and recognized a person who had laughed easily, who had moved through crowds without hesitation, and he understood why he felt permanently humiliated. The shame was not about the event itself, but about the way it had settled into his routine, a quiet verdict that seemed to follow him into every room. He had stopped trying to explain the shift to his colleagues, who simply noted his thoroughness and his quiet demeanor. What frightened him most now was the persistence of these experiences, the way the avoided spaces and guarded glances simply filled his days without demanding his attention. He sought help now because the tightness in his chest had begun to echo in his sleep, and the scent of citrus and starch no longer felt like a passing memory but like a warning he could no longer ignore. He hoped, he told himself, that he might learn to move through a room without measuring the distance to the door, that he might find his way back to the man who had once been happy, before the door caught behind him and changed everything.
